title: Confucius never heard the name Confucius: Jesuits coined it 2,000 years after he died

cover.alt: A large hall of the Temple of Confucius in Qufu, Shandong, China, with a sweeping tiled roof.

body: The teacher known in the West as Confucius was Kong Qiu (c. 551–479 BCE), called by his followers Kongzi or Kongfuzi, ‘Master Kong’. The Latin form ‘Confucius’ was coined in the late 16th century by Jesuit missionaries in China, and in 1687 Jesuits in Paris published Confucius Sinarum Philosophus, ‘Confucius, Philosopher of the Chinese’, a translation of Confucian works with an overview of Chinese history. Even the Analects, the collection of sayings we quote in his name, was compiled by disciples and followers many years after his death.

slides.heading: Match the name to what it is
slides.explanation: Kong was the family name and Qiu the given name; Zhongni was his courtesy name. Kongfuzi became ‘Confucius’ in the late 16th century.

slides.heading: Why Latin?
slides.text: Latin was the shared language of European scholars, so missionaries Latinised Chinese names the way they Latinised their own. The 1687 volume, by Prospero Intorcetta, Philippe Couplet and two colleagues, gave European readers a translation of Confucian works together with an overview of Chinese history.

slides.label: covered by the Cemetery of Confucius in Qufu, his home town
slides.text: The cemetery, Kong Lin, is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

slides.question: Who wrote down the Analects?
options: His disciples, years after he died
slides.explanation: Sayings about his teachings were compiled in the Analects by disciples and followers, but not until many years after his death.
